note: Front is the prompt, back is the keyed answer. Term-pair cards exist because the exam's favourite trick is swapping two definitions that sound alike.

cards.front: Name all seven ITIL guiding principles.
cards.back: Focus on value · Start where you are · Progress iteratively with feedback · Collaborate and promote visibility · Think and work holistically · Keep it simple and practical · Optimize and automate.

cards.front: Guiding principle: 'Focus on value' — what does it require?
cards.back: Everything the organization does must link back, directly or indirectly, to value for stakeholders. Know who the service consumer is and understand their actual experience, not just your metrics.

cards.front: Guiding principle: 'Start where you are' — what does it require?
cards.back: Do not scrap and rebuild by reflex. Observe and measure the current state directly; existing services, people, and processes usually contain reusable value. Measure what is really there, not what reports claim.

cards.front: Guiding principle: 'Progress iteratively with feedback' — what does it require?
cards.back: Break work into smaller, timeboxed sections that each finish and deliver something usable. Build feedback loops in before, during, and after each iteration.

cards.front: Guiding principle: 'Collaborate and promote visibility' — what does it require?
cards.back: Involve the right people, and make work and its consequences visible. Poor visibility drives poor decisions and hidden work. Cooperation beats hand-offs over a wall.

cards.front: Guiding principle: 'Think and work holistically' — what does it require?
cards.back: No service, practice, or component stands alone. Consider all four dimensions and the whole value stream — optimizing one part in isolation commonly degrades the system.

cards.front: Guiding principle: 'Keep it simple and practical' — what does it require?
cards.back: Use the minimum number of steps to reach the objective and eliminate anything that produces no value. Design for the majority; handle exceptions as exceptions. Outcome-based thinking.

cards.front: Guiding principle: 'Optimize and automate' — what is the ORDER, and why?
cards.back: Optimize first, then automate. Automating an unoptimized process just makes the waste run faster. Automate where it adds value, not everywhere technically possible.

cards.front: Name the four dimensions of service management.
cards.back: 1. Organizations and people  2. Information and technology  3. Partners and suppliers  4. Value streams and processes. All four must be considered for every service, and all four are affected by external PESTLE factors.

cards.front: Dimension: 'Organizations and people' covers what?
cards.back: Structures, roles and responsibilities, culture, staffing, competence. Includes whether the culture actually supports the way of working, not just the org chart.

cards.front: Dimension: 'Information and technology' covers what?
cards.back: The information the service creates and manages, and the technologies supporting it — plus the knowledge, security and compliance requirements attached to that information.

cards.front: Dimension: 'Partners and suppliers' covers what?
cards.back: Relationships with other organizations involved in the design, development, deployment, delivery, support or continual improvement of services. Contracts, agreements, and the organization's sourcing strategy.

cards.front: Dimension: 'Value streams and processes' covers what?
cards.back: How the parts of the organization work in an integrated, coordinated way to enable value creation — the sequence of activities (value stream) and the defined sets of activities that turn inputs into outputs (processes).

cards.front: What external factors affect all four dimensions?
cards.back: PESTLE: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental. The organization does not control them but must account for them.

cards.front: Name the six service value chain activities.
cards.back: Plan · Improve · Engage · Design and transition · Obtain/build · Deliver and support. They interconnect in many different combinations to form value streams; the order is not fixed.

cards.front: Value chain activity 'Plan' — purpose?
cards.back: To ensure a shared understanding of the vision, current status, and improvement direction for all four dimensions and all products and services across the organization.

cards.front: Value chain activity 'Improve' — purpose?
cards.back: To ensure continual improvement of products, services, and practices across all value chain activities and all four dimensions.

cards.front: Value chain activity 'Engage' — purpose?
cards.back: To provide a good understanding of stakeholder needs, transparency, and continual engagement and good relationships with all stakeholders.

cards.front: Value chain activity 'Design and transition' — purpose?
cards.back: To ensure products and services continually meet stakeholder expectations for quality, cost, and time to market.

cards.front: Value chain activity 'Obtain/build' — purpose?
cards.back: To ensure service components are available when and where they are needed, and that they meet agreed specifications.

cards.front: Value chain activity 'Deliver and support' — purpose?
cards.back: To ensure services are delivered and supported according to agreed specifications and stakeholder expectations.

cards.front: List the seven steps of the continual improvement model, in order.
cards.back: 1. What is the vision?  2. Where are we now?  3. Where do we want to be?  4. How do we get there?  5. Take action.  6. Did we get there?  7. How do we keep the momentum going?

cards.front: Continual improvement model — step 1?
cards.back: What is the vision? Link the improvement to the organization's vision and objectives, translated for the business unit doing the work.

cards.front: Continual improvement model — step 2, and why it is the step that gets skipped?
cards.back: Where are we now? The baseline. Measure the current state honestly. Skip it and you cannot answer step 6 ('Did we get there?') — you have no evidence improvement happened.

cards.front: Continual improvement model — step 3?
cards.back: Where do we want to be? Define the target state as measurable objectives, agreed with stakeholders.

cards.front: Continual improvement model — step 4?
cards.back: How do we get there? Plan the route — often best done as iterations rather than one big-bang plan.

cards.front: Continual improvement model — step 5?
cards.back: Take action. Execute the improvement, which may be a project, an iteration, or an experiment.

cards.front: Continual improvement model — step 6?
cards.back: Did we get there? Check the measurements against the baseline and the target. Confirm progress, or accept the approach did not work and re-plan.

cards.front: Continual improvement model — step 7?
cards.back: How do we keep the momentum going? Embed and sustain the improvement, market the success, and reinforce the behaviours so it does not decay.

cards.front: Who is responsible for continual improvement?
cards.back: Everyone in the organization. A dedicated role or team may coordinate it, but responsibility is organization-wide and leadership must visibly commit to it.

cards.front: Incident vs problem — the distinction.
cards.back: An INCIDENT is an unplanned interruption to a service or reduction in its quality; the goal is to restore service as fast as possible. A PROBLEM is a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents; the goal is to reduce likelihood and impact by understanding the cause. Restoration is never held hostage to root cause analysis.

cards.front: Problem vs known error — the distinction.
cards.back: A PROBLEM is the cause (or potential cause) of incidents, still under analysis. A KNOWN ERROR is a problem that HAS been analysed but is not yet resolved — typically it has a documented workaround. Known errors are managed under error control.

cards.front: What is an event, and how does it differ from an incident?
cards.back: An EVENT is any change of state significant to the management of a service or CI. Events may be informational, a warning, or an exception. Only some events are incidents — a clean failover that users never notice is an event, not an incident.

cards.front: Service request vs incident — the distinction.
cards.back: A SERVICE REQUEST is a request from a user for something normal, pre-defined and pre-authorized — access, information, a standard provisioning action. An INCIDENT is unplanned and unwanted. Requests should be standardized and automated wherever possible; nothing is broken.

cards.front: What is a workaround, and does it close the problem?
cards.back: A workaround is a solution that reduces or eliminates the impact of an incident or problem for which a full resolution is not yet available. It lets the incident be closed. It does NOT resolve the problem — the problem stays open as a known error.

cards.front: Release vs deployment — the distinction.
cards.back: DEPLOYMENT management moves new or changed hardware, software, documentation, or processes into a live environment. RELEASE management makes new or changed features AVAILABLE FOR USE. A feature flag switched off in production is deployed but not released.

cards.front: Utility vs warranty — which is which?
cards.back: UTILITY = fitness for PURPOSE — what the service does, the functionality it offers. WARRANTY = fitness for USE — how well it performs: availability, capacity, security, continuity. Both are required for value. The exam's favourite trap is reversing them.

cards.front: Output vs outcome — the distinction.
cards.back: An OUTPUT is a tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity. An OUTCOME is a result for a stakeholder, ENABLED by one or more outputs. Shipping every planned feature is outputs; nobody adopting it means the outcome never landed.

cards.front: Standard vs normal vs emergency change.
cards.back: STANDARD: low risk, pre-authorized, well understood, fully documented — authorized once when the procedure was created, no per-instance approval. NORMAL: scheduled, assessed and authorized through the change model, may go to a CAB. EMERGENCY: must be implemented immediately (usually to restore service); expedited authority such as an ECAB, documentation may follow the fix.

cards.front: Change enablement — purpose (exact emphasis matters).
cards.back: To MAXIMIZE THE NUMBER OF SUCCESSFUL SERVICE AND PRODUCT CHANGES by ensuring risks are properly assessed, authorizing changes to proceed, and managing the change schedule. Note: maximize successful changes — not minimize or restrict changes.

cards.front: How does ITIL 4 define value?
cards.back: The perceived benefits, usefulness, and importance of something. 'Perceived' is the operative word — value is judged by the stakeholder, not asserted by the provider.

cards.front: How do costs and risks work in a service relationship?
cards.back: Services REMOVE some costs and risks from the consumer (the provider carries them) and IMPOSE others on the consumer (fees, adoption effort, dependence on the provider). Both directions are examined.

cards.front: What is a 'service', and what is a 'service offering'?
cards.back: A SERVICE is a means of enabling value co-creation by facilitating outcomes customers want, without the customer managing specific costs and risks. A SERVICE OFFERING is a formal description of one or more services designed for a target consumer group — may include goods, access to resources, and service actions.

cards.front: What are the components of the ITIL service value system?
cards.back: Guiding principles · Governance · Service value chain · Practices · Continual improvement. Inputs are opportunity and demand; the output is value. Its purpose is to ensure the organization co-creates value consistently.

cards.front: Service level management — purpose, and the 'watermelon effect'.
cards.back: Purpose: set clear BUSINESS-BASED targets for service performance so delivery can be assessed, monitored, and managed against them. The watermelon effect: every technical metric is green on the outside while the user experience is red on the inside — which is why SLAs must relate to defined outcomes, not component metrics.

cards.front: Service desk — purpose.
cards.back: To capture demand for incident resolution and service requests, and to act as the single point of contact between the service provider and all of its users. It is the entry point, not necessarily the fulfiller.

cards.front: What is 'service management'?
cards.back: A set of specialized organizational capabilities for enabling value to customers in the form of services. Key phrase: specialized organizational capabilities.

cards.front: Customer vs user vs sponsor — the three consumer roles.
cards.back: CUSTOMER defines requirements and is accountable for outcomes. USER is a person who uses services. SPONSOR authorizes budget for service consumption. One person can hold all three roles, or they can be separate people.

cards.front: What is an 'organization' in ITIL 4?
cards.back: A person or a group of people that has its own functions with responsibilities, authorities, and relationships to achieve its objectives. Note: can be a single person.

cards.front: What is 'risk' in ITIL 4?
cards.back: A possible event that could cause harm or loss, or make it more difficult to achieve objectives. Risk can also relate to positive outcomes (opportunities).

cards.front: Service provision vs service consumption vs service relationship management.
cards.back: SERVICE PROVISION: provider-side activities (managing resources, fulfilling actions). SERVICE CONSUMPTION: consumer-side activities (managing resources needed to use the service). SERVICE RELATIONSHIP MANAGEMENT: joint activities by both sides to ensure continual value co-creation.

cards.front: Utility and warranty — full official definitions.
cards.back: UTILITY: the functionality offered by a product or service to meet a particular need. Shorthand: fitness for purpose. WARRANTY: the assurance that a product or service will meet agreed requirements. Shorthand: fitness for use. Both required for value.

cards.front: Are the guiding principles mandatory or optional?
cards.back: They are RECOMMENDATIONS — not mandatory rules — that guide an organization in all circumstances. They should NEVER be changed or discarded, regardless of changes in goals, strategy, or structure.

cards.front: Optimization vs automation — the distinction and the three-step sequence.
cards.back: OPTIMIZATION: improving efficiency by removing waste. AUTOMATION: using technology with minimal human involvement. Sequence: (1) understand what can be improved, (2) eliminate unnecessary steps, (3) automate what remains. Always optimize BEFORE automating.

cards.front: What is an information radiator, and which principle does it map to?
cards.back: An Agile visibility tool (task board, dashboard, big visible chart) that broadcasts work status without anyone having to ask. Maps to 'collaborate and promote visibility'.

cards.front: Name the four service desk models.
cards.back: LOCAL: co-located with users. CENTRALIZED: fewer locations serving a larger user base. VIRTUAL: staff in any location, technology makes them appear as one desk. FOLLOW-THE-SUN: 24-hour coverage across time zones, each zone hands off to the next.

cards.front: Three valid SLA data sources (and one trap).
cards.back: Valid: (1) customer feedback and surveys, (2) business-related metrics, (3) operational metrics. TRAP: competitor benchmarks are NOT a valid SLA data source.

cards.front: Activities in the 'problem identification' phase.
cards.back: Trend analysis of incident records, detecting duplicate and recurring incidents, analysing information from other practices. TRAP: logging individual incidents is incident management, not problem identification.

cards.front: Is 'routine' a type of change in ITIL 4?
cards.back: NO. 'Routine' is NOT a change type. The three types are: STANDARD (pre-authorized, low risk), NORMAL (scheduled, assessed, authorized), EMERGENCY (expedited for urgent restoration or security). 'Routine' is a common exam trap.

cards.front: Who can report an incident?
cards.back: ANYONE — users, technical staff, or automated monitoring tools. Not limited to end users or the service desk.

cards.front: SLM contributions to all 6 value chain activities.
cards.back: PLAN: actual performance data and trends. ENGAGE: collects/processes customer and user feedback. DESIGN & TRANSITION: feeds customer feedback into new/changed services. OBTAIN/BUILD: provides performance objectives for components. DELIVER & SUPPORT: communicates targets to ops, collects interaction feedback. IMPROVE: uses feedback to make services better.

cards.front: Service request management contributions to 5 value chain activities.
cards.back: ENGAGE: collects user requirements, sets expectations, provides status. OBTAIN/BUILD: acquires pre-approved components. DESIGN & TRANSITION: initiates standard changes. DELIVER & SUPPORT: keeps users productive. IMPROVE: provides trend, quality, and feedback data.
